title: Pregnant patient with resistant hypertension and severe hypokalemia
vignette: A pregnant patient with hypertension is found to have severe hypokalemia. First-line management of the presumed underlying condition is limited in pregnancy because the standard drug of choice carries a fetal risk. Build your workup and management plan.
questions_for_student: What secondary cause of hypertension should severe hypokalemia in pregnancy make you consider?
Why is spironolactone avoided in pregnancy, and what can be used instead?
If medical therapy fails, when in pregnancy is surgery safest?

expert_nodes.label: Ask about pre-existing hypertension and prior pregnancies
expert_nodes.rationale: Chronic HTN + hypokalemia in pregnancy should raise suspicion for a secondary cause, not just gestational HTN

expert_nodes.label: Serum potassium + basic metabolic panel
expert_nodes.rationale: Reveals severe hypokalemia, the key clue pointing away from routine gestational hypertension

expert_nodes.label: Plasma aldosterone / renin ratio (adapted for pregnancy)
expert_nodes.rationale: Confirms primary aldosteronism despite pregnancy-related RAAS changes complicating interpretation

expert_nodes.label: Adrenal imaging (MRI preferred in pregnancy)
expert_nodes.rationale: Localizes the aldosterone-producing adenoma while avoiding ionizing radiation

expert_nodes.label: Avoid spironolactone; consider eplerenone instead
expert_nodes.rationale: Spironolactone is contraindicated in pregnancy due to anti-androgenic effects on the fetus

expert_nodes.label: Start eplerenone as a short-term bridge
expert_nodes.rationale: Controls hypokalemia/hypertension medically while definitive treatment is planned

expert_nodes.label: Reassess if refractory to medical therapy
expert_nodes.rationale: Determines whether surgery is needed before term

expert_nodes.label: Unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy in the second trimester
expert_nodes.rationale: Second trimester is the safest surgical window in pregnancy; addresses the source directly once medical therapy is insufficient

expert_nodes.label: Primary aldosteronism secondary to adrenal adenoma
expert_nodes.rationale: Working diagnosis established once biochemical and imaging findings converge

case_source.consent_note: Published case report — de-identification and consent handled by the journal prior to publication

citation.authors: Lin A, Chan SJ, Crapanzano JP, Kuo EJ
citation.title: Severe hypokalaemia in primary aldosteronism during pregnancy

follow_up.actual_path: In the published case, eplerenone was used as a short-term bridge to control severe hypokalemia after spironolactone was ruled out due to pregnancy. When the patient remained refractory to medical management, a unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy was performed in the second trimester.
follow_up.complications: None reported to the fetus from eplerenone use, per the published abstract.
follow_up.discharge_outcome: Not detailed in the publicly available abstract — see full article for exact discharge status.
follow_up.long_term: Not detailed in the publicly available abstract — see full article for follow-up data.
follow_up.teaching_pearl: Severe hypokalemia in a hypertensive pregnant patient should not be assumed to be routine gestational hypertension — it's a red flag for a secondary cause like primary aldosteronism, and the standard first-line drug (spironolactone) is off the table in pregnancy.
